name: Lemon and sugar lip lightening

lead: Some people rub lemon juice, often mixed with sugar, onto their lips hoping to lighten them and slough off dry skin for a smoother, lighter look.
Proponents credit the acidity of lemon, which is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid, and the abrasion of sugar. No published study of the mixture for lip pigmentation was identified.

paras: It is a home routine: juice and sugar are mixed, rubbed gently on the lips and rinsed off, usually repeated over days or weeks. People often follow it with a lip balm.

Contact with citrus juice followed by sunlight can cause phytophotodermatitis, with redness, blistering and lasting brown marks, because plant compounds such as furanocoumarins sensitize skin to UVA. Lips are thin skin, and lemon acid can sting on chapped or cracked areas.

angle.text: DIY posters rub lemon juice and sugar on the lips hoping to lighten them. The idea is that the acid fades pigment while the sugar exfoliates, leaving lighter lips. It is a home-remedy belief, and no study has looked at it for lip color.

lead: Lemon and sugar lip lightening is a home remedy in which lemon juice, usually combined with sugar granules, is applied to or rubbed on the lips with the aim of making them lighter.
Lemon juice contains roughly 5 to 6 percent citric acid.[1] No published study of the mixture for lip pigmentation was identified.

Dermatology sources describe a reaction called phytophotodermatitis, in which light-sensitizing plant compounds such as furanocoumarins on the skin plus UVA exposure cause inflammation and later pigmentation.[2]

paras: Proponents describe gentle scrubbing of the lips with the mixture. The thin lip skin has only three to five cell layers, versus up to sixteen on typical facial skin.[3]

Phytophotodermatitis follows contact with a light-sensitizing botanical such as lime juice and then sun exposure. Symptoms appear within a day, peak at 48 to 72 hours, and can include blisters. Healing may leave dark marks that last several years.[2] The article names lime as the best-known source; lemon juice is not specifically described in the sources consulted.
